column4: The source section labels ل ه م as its root for ilham and pictures a thing cast inward and swallowed; 16:68 says “أَوْحَىٰ رَبُّكَ إِلَى النَّحْلِ,” giving a concrete divine instruction received by an animal. The next ayah completes this bee scene with its drink.

The section’s root ل ه م frames inspiration as something placed within; here Allah inspires Moses’ mother to nurse him and then cast him into the river. The verse joins inward divine instruction to the section’s concrete image of a young creature taking nourishment from its mother.

The source section’s root ل ه م describes Allah placing something in the inner self; here Allah says He inspired the disciples to believe in Him and His messenger. This gives the inner reception a specific moral content, faith, alongside the section’s fujur and taqwa.

This continues the inspired-bee scene of 16:68; its own contribution is that a drink comes from the bees’ bellies and is healing for people. It makes the section’s meeting of inward reception, animal life, and drink concrete in one passage.

The section says the camel’s suqyā is a protected drinking share; Salih specifies that she has a turn to drink and the people have a known day’s turn. This is the clearest statement of the divided water right that the section reads in “وَسُقْيَٰهَا.”

The source section’s root س ق ي includes setting drink aside for someone to take; here the water is explicitly “قِسْمَةٌۢ بَيْنَهُمْ,” with each drinking turn attended. It turns the camel’s protected share into an explicit allocation.

The commentary hears nafs as a sip and water as what sustains it; in this scene water springs from the rock and each group knows its own drinking place. The verse adds a communal arrangement of access to the life-sustaining drink.

This parallel account says twelve springs burst forth and each group knew its drinking place. The source section’s image of the camel’s assigned water share is set beside an orderly distribution that gives every group a known place.

This is Salih’s warning about Allah’s she-camel: leave her to graze on Allah’s land and do not touch her with harm. It makes explicit the protective force of the short command “نَاقَةَ ٱللَّهِ وَسُقْيَٰهَا” in the source section.

Salih identifies the she-camel as a sign, tells his people to let her graze on Allah’s land, and forbids harming her. This spells out the warning carried by the section’s elliptical “camel of Allah and her drinking.”
Here the she-camel is sent as a trial for Thamud, and they are told to watch and wait. The next verse, 54:28, specifies the divided water share central to the source image.

After 26:155 assigns the camel and people their drinking turns, Salih forbids them to harm her and warns of punishment. This verse shows the boundary protecting the share described in the preceding ayah.

The people hamstring the camel, and Salih tells them they have only three days before the promised punishment. This is the direct counterpart to 91:14’s hamstringing and destruction; 11:64 supplies the preceding warning about the camel.
The people hamstring the camel after Salih’s warning about her drinking in 26:155 and 26:156. This is the same violation and action named in 91:14; 26:158 gives the resulting punishment.
The people call their companion, who takes up the task and hamstrings the camel. This supplies the agent and act compressed into 91:14; the preceding 54:28 has assigned the water share they violate.
The people hamstring the camel, reject Salih’s command, and challenge him to bring the punishment. This is a close parallel to 91:14’s denial and killing; the next verse gives the destruction.
Punishment overtakes the people after they hamstring the camel in 26:157. The verse supplies the consequence corresponding to “فَدَمْدَمَ عَلَيْهِمْ” in 91:14.
After 54:30’s warning about punishment, this verse says Allah sent a single blast and the people became like dry stalks. It gives the specific aftermath to the destruction compressed in 91:14.
After the camel is hamstrung in 11:65, a blast seizes the wrongdoers. The verse gives the immediate destruction corresponding to the Lord’s action in 91:14; 11:68 states the lasting desolation.
This continues the destruction in 11:67 by saying they were as though they had never lived there. It makes the totalizing force of 91:14’s “فَسَوَّىٰهَا” concrete in the parallel Thamud account.
The earthquake seizes the people after they hamstring the camel in 7:77, leaving them fallen in their homes. It completes the same warning, violation, and destruction sequence as 91:13 and 91:14.

The source section explicitly labels ذ ن ب as the root and reads ذَنُوب as a full bucket and a share; 51:59 uses “ذَنُوبًا” for the wrongdoers’ share like that of earlier peoples. Its own wording turns sin into an allotted portion; the preceding 51:43, 51:44, and 51:45 names Thamud and their destruction, connecting that comparison to the people in 91.

The source section presents the she-camel as Allah’s protected sign and recounts that Thamud killed her; 17:59 likewise names the she-camel of Thamud as a visible sign and says they wronged her. It makes the camel’s sign-status explicit while connecting mistreatment of her with rejection of a sign.

The source section says Thamud denied the messenger before hamstringing the camel; 54:23 states that Thamud denied the warnings. This verse supplies the rejection that leads into the camel trial in 54:27 and the water division in 54:28.

Here Thamud object that they should follow one human among themselves, a concrete form of rejecting Salih as messenger. It sharpens the denial summarized in 91:14; 54:27, 54:28, and 54:29 then show the camel, her share, and the violation.

Thamud ask whether the reminder was sent to him alone and call him a liar. This specifies what their denial of the messenger entails in the source section; 54:27, 54:28, and 54:29 continue with the camel and her drinking share.

The people tell Salih that he is bewitched, a specific refusal of the messenger whom 91:14 says they denied. The next verse demands a sign, and 26:155, 26:156, and 26:157 give the camel’s water share and their attack on her.

Thamud demand a sign from Salih if he is truthful; this leads directly to the camel’s specified drinking turn in 26:155. It connects rejection of the messenger to the protected sign at the center of the source image.

This ayah points readers to the terrible punishment and warnings after the camel is hamstrung in 54:29; 54:31 supplies what happened, one blast and dry stalks. Its own contribution is the warning that follows the act, echoing the consequence named in 91:14 and the lack of fear in 91:15.

This verse warns that the people will learn who the liar is, immediately before the camel is sent as a trial in 54:27. It connects the source section’s denial and punishment to the trial that follows.

The source section distinguishes its root ل ه م, an inward casting, from ordinary outward speech; 2:97 describes Gabriel bringing revelation to the Prophet’s heart by Allah’s permission. The verse gives a parallel of divine communication reaching the inner person, though its Qur’anic revelation is not the same claim as the section’s ilham.

The section’s dictionary branch for ن ف س says water is called nafs because the soul depends on it; 21:30 says every living thing was made from water. This makes the commentary’s water-as-condition-of-life association concrete beyond thirst.

The source section’s root س ق ي concerns giving someone drink, and its camel is allowed to graze; 16:10 brings together water for people to drink and pasture for animals. It joins the same two necessities that surround the camel’s protected share.

The section’s ن ف س dictionary note ties the soul’s standing to water; 25:49 describes rain reviving dead land and giving drink to many animals and people. It places the camel’s ration within water as shared provision for living creatures.

The source section identifies س ق ي as giving someone what they drink; 15:22 says “فَأَسْقَيْنَاكُمُوهُ,” presenting rainwater as something given to drink. It clarifies the provision side of the camel’s allotted drink.
The source section develops drinking as a measured share; 23:18 says water is sent down “بِقَدَرٍ” and can be taken away. This makes explicit both the measure of water provision and its boundary.

Salih’s camel is permitted to graze on Allah’s land and has a protected water turn; 79:31 pairs the earth’s water with its pasture. The verse brings together the two resources that the camel scene allocates and protects.

This verse calls the water and pasture in the preceding creation sequence provision for people and their livestock. It makes the camel’s grazing and drinking share part of the wider provision given to humans and animals.

The source section’s dictionary example is an unweaned young animal taking milk from its mother; 28:12 says Moses had been refused wet nurses before his own mother was brought to nurse him. This continues 28:7’s command to nurse him and completes the parallel feeding scene.

The section’s ل ه م dictionary example is a young creature taking all it needs from its mother’s udder; 2:233 describes mothers nursing children for up to two complete years and assigns their provision to the father. It gives a human parallel in which nourishment and its allotted support are explicit.

The source section says the self receives both fujur and taqwa; 76:3 says the human is shown the way and may be grateful or ungrateful. The verse makes the inner moral alternatives legible as contrasting responses.

The section’s fujur and taqwa name two moral directions received by the self; 90:10 says God showed the human being the two ways. This gives the paired inner orientations an image of alternatives made visible.

The section’s paired fujur and taqwa lead into the people’s chosen wrong against the camel; 17:7 states that doing good benefits the self and doing evil is against it. It makes the consequence of moral direction return to the person who takes it.

The source section pictures the self receiving its moral qualities and Thamud receiving a share for their wrong; 2:286 says a soul has what it earns and bears what it acquires. This links inner moral capacity with personal accountability.

The source section says Allah inspires the self with both fujur and taqwa; 4:79 says good is from Allah while evil is from the self. This is a specific theological boundary on how the two inner orientations are attributed, illuminating the difference between receiving a capacity and owning one’s deed.

The source section describes the self as formed and receiving both moral directions; 30:30 describes people as created upon Allah’s fitrah. This offers a boundary on the moral image: a created disposition toward God is set beside the section’s account of both fujur and taqwa.

The source section labels ر س ل as the root of رسول and cites the secondary dictionary form رَسْل for abundant, successive milk; 47:15 pictures rivers of milk in Paradise. This is a specific milk-flow echo through the source’s dictionary branch, though the ayah itself uses لبن and does not call a messenger milk.

The source section’s dictionary branch رَسْل links رسول with abundant milk; 16:66 describes pure milk from livestock as a drink. This supplies a concrete animal-milk scene for that secondary association, though the ayah itself does not use the root ر س ل.
